newsitem.title: USA: GPU eyeing Oyster Creek sale or closure.
newsitem.headline: GPU eyeing Oyster Creek sale or closure.

text.p: GPU Inc said Thursday it is exploring the sale or early retirement of the Oyster Creek Nuclear Generating Station to mitigate costs associated with continued operation of the plant.

As part of its July 15 restructuring filing with the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities, GPU said plans to propose the two options in addition to continued operation of the 619-megawatt boiling water reactor located on the Barnegat Bay in Ocean County, N.J.
The filing will not consider the sale or early retirement of Three Mile Island Unit 1, the company said.
Owned by GPU's Jersey Central Power & Light Co subsidiary and operated by GPU Nuclear Inc Oyster Creek began commercial operation in 1969 and is licensed to operate until 2009.
If a decision is made to retire the plant early, retirement would likely take place in about 2000.
Any opportunities for the sale of Oyster Creek to third parties during this period will be reviewed, GPU said.

"I would not anticipate an increase in rates for our New Jersey customers. A rate decrease could occur upon the successful replacement of Oyster Creek's energy with a lower-cost source," GPU President Dennis Baldassari said.
"The electricity generated at Oyster Creek costs GPU Energy about $0.015 more per kilowatthour than the current market price for energy," GPU's statement said without elaborating.

Baldassair said the current rate structure would be adequate to collect GPU's net investment in the plant and provide for decommissioning costs, as well as for replacement energy and capacity if Oyster Creek is retired.
He is confident that GPU would be able to offset the 619 megawatts of Oyster Creek capacity with additional, New Jersey-based capacity and/or transmission system enhancements.
"In response to the increasingly competitive market for electricity generation, GPU has been reviewing its generation assets more closely," Baldassari said.
Last year, for example, GPU closed the 72-megawatt Gilbert Unit 3 and 58-megawatt Werner Unit 4 fossil-fueled units because their costs were above the current market prices.
Assuming the plant is not sold, decommissioning Oyster Creek would probably be accomplished by the "prompt removal/dismantlement method," GPU Nuclear chief executive T. Gary Broughton said.
This means the process will begin immediately after the plant is retired.

He said this option is more cost-effective than placing the plant in monitored storage and other options that delay the start of the process. Decommissioning is expected to last several years, at a projected cost of some $400 million.
